No new information revealed by opponent I announce that I’m casting Common Sense, and place it in my cemetery. Before searching my deck, I change my mind and take it back. I return Common Sense to my hand, and have not cast the spell. Searching your own deck I play Common Sense and start to look through my deck. At this point, takebacks are no longer possible. Even though I theoretically knew all the cards in my deck and I’m potentially not gaining new information, it would be too burdensome to shuffle your deck and remember the position of any cards previously seen, including any mulligan’ed cards. Therefore, for speed of play and consistency, once you start looking at your deck to search, takebacks aren’t allowed. Collection I look at my collection during the game. This does not influence takebacks in any way, since that’s information already available to me, and the order doesn’t matter. New information revealed by opponent I announce that I’m attacking your site with my Petrosian Cavalry. You could Defend with your Vile Imp, but you decline. Once you decline to Defend, I can no longer take back my attack (or anything that occurred prior to that attack), since you revealed the information that you wouldn’t Defend, which was previously unknown to me. Mandatory Triggered Abilities I announce that I’m summoning my Apprentice Wizard to my Colour out of Space. The spell resolves, and before I draw my spell, you alert me that your Shark is going to come fight my Wizard, since the Colour out of Space is a water site in your Shark’s body of water. No new information has been revealed, since that is a mandatory trigger. I would be allowed to take back my casting of the Apprentice Wizard, and perhaps summon it to a different location or not at all. Note: If I had drawn a spell and then we realized the Shark issue, the players should call a judge, since a game rule was broken (the Shark resolves before the card draw). The judge would then talk with both players and decide how to fix the rules error (potentially giving both players a warning, since both players are responsible for properly following the game rules). Passive Abilities, No new information I place my Tower nearby a Smokestacks of Gnaak, then I try to cast a spell requiring an extra mana. You alert me that I don’t have that much mana, because the Smokestacks negated the genesis ability. I take back my spell, and I can also take back my Tower, playing it in a different square, or playing a different site entirely. Multiple Actions, No new information I cast Seven-League Boots to my Megamoeba. Then, my Megamoeba uses Move and Attack, stepping in multiple ways, including trying to move over a Perilous Bridge. My opponent points out that I can't move the Megamoeba over the Perilous Bridge. We know exactly what locations the Megamoeba occupied before Move and Attack, so we take back to that point. I realize that I don't want to cast my Seven-League Boots either, so I take that back too. Forgetting to Tap Your Avatar to Draw a Site Sometimes a player will forget to tap their avatar to draw a site and end their turn with their avatar untapped. Normal takeback rules apply: As long as no new information has been revealed, it’s fine to take back and let them tap to draw a site. Note that the opponent choosing to draw a site or spell at the start of their turn is new information, and technically would prohibit takebacks after that. Nonetheless, please be cool and if it’s obvious your opponent would have tapped to draw a site, please allow it. Defender Taking Back their Choice to Defend If the active player declares an attack, then the defender chooses to defend, and then no new information or action is revealed by the attacking player, the defender may take back their defending choice. For example: I attack your site with my Daperyll Vampire. You defend with your Foot Soldier. I kill your Foot Soldier and heal 4 life; at that moment, before I’ve had a chance to declare any other actions, you decide that you want to take back the Foot Soldier’s defense so that I don’t heal. That’s fine! Notes: • If the defending player takes back their defending choice, the attacker will also have an opportunity to further take back their attack! • If the acting player declares further actions (or ends their turn) after the defend choice, it is too late to take back, since new information was revealed. • If there are multiple units involved in defending, once the attacker splits up damage between all the defending units, new information has been revealed and it’s too late to take back.

Some judging situations are straightforward: the rulebook, FAQs, or Codex provide a clear answer. Others are more difficult. A player may accidentally cast a spell without the required threshold, forget an ongoing effect, draw extra cards, or make another honest mistake that is only discovered several turns later. Both players share responsibility for maintaining a legal game state. Encourage players to help each other remember thresholds, ongoing effects, and other game rules. Nevertheless, mistakes will happen. When they do, players should call a judge immediately. Your role is not to mechanically apply a penalty. Your role is to restore fairness. When evaluating a tricky situation: • Listen carefully to both players and ensure they feel heard. • Rewind the game state to the point of the error, if this can be done cleanly and fairly. • If rewinding is not practical, use your judgment to adjust the game state so that no player benefits from the illegal action. • Consult other judges whenever helpful. The exact remedy will vary from situation to situation. You may choose to rewind fully, partially rewind, compensate one player for lost information or advantage, or apply another fair solution. There is intentionally no exhaustive list of remedies. The important principles are: • Honest mistakes should not provide an advantage. • Honest mistakes should not be punished more harshly than necessary. • Players should be left feeling that they were treated fairly and respectfully. If a player intentionally breaks the rules to gain an advantage, that is cheating and should be treated accordingly. Above all, remember: your goal is not to achieve a perfect reconstruction of the game. Your goal is to preserve the integrity of the competition while protecting the player experience. We trust your judgment. Example: Casting Grandmaster Wizard Without Sufficient Threshold Ira casts Grandmaster Wizard with only 1 air threshold. Neither player notices the mistake. Ira draws three cards, and ends his turn. David takes his turn, doing several things, including killing the Grandmaster Wizard. Ira starts his next turn, draws a card, plays a Tower, and then realizes the mistake. The players call a judge. At this point, some tournament rules might try to give a definitive answer, but Sorcery tournament rules say simply that “the judge uses their judgment to make things fair.” Most importantly, you should talk to the players to find out what they think is fair, and what they would want to happen. Ensure that both players feel equally heard. After that discussion, here are some examples of what you might decide (not an exhaustive list): Solution 1. Full Rewind Since Ira knows what 4 cards he drew (3 from Grandmaster + 1 from start of this turn), and David’s actions are easy enough to revert, it’s possible to rewind. Therefore, the game is rewound to the point where Ira illegally played Grandmaster Wizard, life totals are updated, sites are returned to hand, etc. Ira’s four extra cards are shuffled into his deck. The judge decides that David gets to keep the card he drew at the start of his turn as compensation for all the information he revealed on his turn. Play continues from Ira’s turn just before playing the Grandmaster Wizard. Why it works: • The illegal action is entirely undone. • The game returns to a legal state. • A minor compensation addresses information revealed during the rewind. Solution 2. Partial Rewind with Compensation Since Ira had the Tower in hand last turn, the judge rules that Ira retroactively played the Tower last turn instead. The Tower is placed in the location of the previous site, and the previous site is returned to Ira’s hand. Ira continues with his current turn and is able to play a site normally now. Even though Ira would have had 1 extra mana last turn from the Tower, he is not allowed to use it retroactively because it might have changed David’s whole turn. Why it works: • The judge does not attempt to fully recreate the game. • A legal alternative game state is substituted. • The judge intentionally limits retroactive benefits to preserve fairness. Solution 3. No Rewind, Compensation Only After David killed Ira’s Grandmaster Wizard, he played Pillars of Zeiros to banish it. This is such significant information revealed that trying to rewind would be too difficult. Therefore, the judge rules that nothing is rewound, but as compensation to David, he gets to immediately draw an extra card. Why it works: • The game state remains exactly as it is. • The judge acknowledges that rewinding would be more disruptive than helpful. • Compensation is used to restore balance instead. The point of these resolutions is that there isn’t a single, definitive way to handle a situation. Any of the bullets above would be correct, if that’s what the judge decided, having listened to the players and used their judgment. There are so many different possibilities about what happened, what can be easily rewound, how the players feel, how much information was gained, how much advantage was received, etc. In the end, we rely on the judge to use their judgment, since we believe that will yield the most fair and fun results. In summary: • Talk with both of the players and understand what they think would be fair. • Rewind if possible. • If rewinding isn’t possible, based on your discussion with the players, adjust the game state so that the illegal play didn’t give any advantage. • Consult with other judges as needed. To avoid all of this, encourage players to pay attention to the game and ensure both players are both following the rules!

Sorcery allows for limited takebacks during your main phase for convenience and to minimize "gotcha" moments. We want everyone to play their best game and have fun, which aligns with the golden rule. These takeback rules are intentionally designed to be reasonably lenient while maintaining a good speed of play. We want to encourage a fun, relaxed environment, even when playing competitively and minimize the number of “gotcha” plays. Takebacks are OK until any of these occur: • New information is revealed by your opponent (e.g. decision to Defend or not, or to end their turn) • A random event resolves • You gain information (drawing a card or looking at a card) • So many actions have resolved that it's too complicated to easily revert the gamestate (call a judge if you are uncertain) Two further notes: • Excessive takebacks can slow down play; if you are concerned, talk with your opponent politely and/or call a judge. • If both players agree freely, you may take back however you wish. It’s important that a player is not pressured to accept takebacks beyond what’s specified here. General Reminder If both players agree to a take back, regardless of anything above, as long as neither player was pressured or coerced in any way, it’s fine to allow a take back. We expect the highest standards of fair play among Sorcery players and cheating does not happen at Sorcery events. We do not tolerate it. Note that players may unintentionally break the game rules, which is not cheating if it was accidental. In the example above, if Ira honestly didn’t realize he lacked the threshold to cast the Grandmaster Wizard, that is a mistake, but not cheating. If he knowingly cast the spell without meeting the threshold, that is cheating. Please note that almost all incidents of this kind of mistake are unintentional. This is where you must use your judgment. This is not an exhaustive list of possible cheating: • Knowingly breaking any game rule. • Using marked cards. • Insufficiently randomized decks. • Mismatched decklist and physical cards. In addition to the Grandmaster Wizard example above (where you would need to decide if Ira knowingly or unknowingly broke the game rule), here’s a marked cards example: • Looking closely at a player’s card sleeves, some are visibly different from others. You ask the player about it and they explain they used some newer and some older sleeves, but it wasn’t intentional. Looking at the cards in those marked sleeves, there doesn’t seem to be a pattern. Therefore, you determine that the player unknowingly used marked sleeves. You direct them to get fresh sleeves, and there is no penalty. • Alternately, you notice that the three marked sleeves are two Sinkholes and Roots of Yggdrasil in a Geomancer deck. The player gives the same explanation as above. Using your judgment, you conclude that the player really did know those sleeves were different and used them anyway, gaining an advantage. That is cheating. Except in the most clear-cut cases, there will likely be some uncertainty between an honest mistake and cheating. As a judge, you are empowered to use your judgment. Multiple cases of “honest mistakes” that consistently advantage the player may point toward cheating. Please discuss cases like this with the head judge. If someone is cheating, they should be disqualified from the event, receive no prizes, and likely be banned from future events. If this ever happens, please notify Erik’s Curiosa by emailing support@sorcerytcg.com.

We recommend at least 1 judge per 32 players you expect to have at your event. If you are expecting: • 33-64 players, plan for at least 2 judges. • 65-96 players, plan for at least 3 judges. • 97-128 players, plan for at least 4 judges. Judges should handle: • rules questions • judge calls during matches • disputes between players • disqualifications, warnings or other sanctions, which should usually not be required • deck checks (ideally you would conduct random deck checks in the back half of the Swiss rounds on the top 2-6 tables, depending on judge capacity). Ideally, you would have a scorekeeper and tournament organiser in addition to these judge positions. The tournament organiser should handle: • announcements to the players about the tournament structure • logistics including prizes, staff breaks, table setup with playmats and table numbers, etc • information for players such as housekeeping, bathrooms, food, etc • answering player questions about any of the above • coordination of scorekeeper, judges, and players to ensure everything is running smoothly. The scorekeeper should: • accept results from players • ensure the results are entered correctly into the software • monitor round time, ensure it is displayed to players and that regular time announcements are made. A Judge's Guide to Sorcery Events

We suggest 50 minutes per game, which should be ample time for the vast majority of Sorcery games played at a reasonable speed. However, you should check with your tournament organizer or staff to confirm how long rounds will take during the event. Use this time you share with your opponent respectfully. A little thinking is fine, but please ensure you are playing reasonably quickly so the game doesn’t reach the time limit. Untimed rounds may occur in finals or decisive matches, as per the tournament organizer’s instructions. These untimed games ensure there is a decisive result, but players are still expected to play at a reasonable pace. If you are still playing when time is called, three bonus turns will be played. Complete the current turn, then start counting turns. For example, if time is called on your turn, you’ll finish your turn. Then, your opponent will take a turn (1), then you (2), then your opponent (3). If the game still isn’t over after the bonus turns, apply these final tiebreakers: • If exactly one player is on Death's Door, they lose. • Otherwise, both players lose. Note: This is entered as a zero-point draw in the play network. We expect a reasonable pace. Judges may intervene if necessary. Time is a shared resource among both players, and each player should strive to use it thoughtfully and evenly. It’s also reasonable to expect that if a player gains substantial new information, they might need some time to adjust. In the end, judges must use their judgment. Judges may apply any remedy they deem appropriate, including warning the player, granting the opponent extra time or bonus turns, applying a game loss, etc.

We want everyone to play their best game and have fun, so Sorcery allows for limited takebacks during your turn to enable timely decision-making during play and minimize 'gotcha' moments. Takebacks are OK until any of these occur: • New information is revealed by your opponent (e.g. decision to Defend or not, or an opponent ending their turn) • A random event resolves • You gain information (drawing a card or looking at a card) • So many actions have resolved that it's too complicated to easily revert the gamestate (call a judge if you are uncertain) If unsure, call a judge.
